narrative:
The model estimates you have a 22% chance of failing your final year, which is high enough that the school requires you to take remedial courses to strengthen your chances of passing.

The prediction is driven mainly by three aspects of your situation. First, you have had no past class failures, which is exactly average for students who passed and strongly pushes the model toward expecting you to succeed. However, two other factors pull the prediction in the opposite direction and outweigh that positive signal. The model sees that you are not receiving extra educational support at school, something the vast majority of successful students also do not need, yet in your specific combination of circumstances this absence of support contributes noticeably toward the risk of failing. Even more influential is that, although you say you want to pursue higher education, the model has learned that students with your overall profile who express this goal but show certain gaps in daily habits and family academic background are still at elevated risk.

To improve, focus on turning your ambition for higher education into concrete daily action. Since you already study 2–5 hours weekly and have only two absences, small consistent changes—such as seeking free tutoring, reducing weekend alcohol consumption that stands out as very high compared with most passers, and using your internet access for structured revision—can shift the balance. These steps address the areas the model flagged as holding you back and can help you move from the “at-risk” group into the group that passes.
